title: Building elements from data
lesson:
In Level 1 you changed elements that were already in the HTML: find one with `getElementById`, set its `textContent`. That works when you know in advance what the page holds. Real apps rarely do. Today's clinic list depends on who walked in; a game's inventory depends on what the player picked up. So the page has to **build elements from data**. Building one element takes four steps: ``` const li = document.createElement("li"); // 1. make it (it exists, but nowhere yet) li.textContent = "maize: 120 kg"; // 2. fill it li.classList.add("big"); // 3. style it (optional) list.appendChild(li); // 4. put it on the page ``` The most common mistake is forgetting step 4: the element is made and filled, but it floats in memory and never appears. If nothing shows up, look for the missing `appendChild`. **textContent or innerHTML?** `innerHTML` reads its string *as HTML*. That's handy for HTML you wrote yourself, but dangerous for data. Suppose a patient's name was typed into a form as ``. Put that into `innerHTML` and the browser builds an image and runs the code. This is called **XSS** (cross-site scripting), and it's one of the most common security holes on the web. `textContent` shows the characters exactly as they are, so the name appears as harmless text. The habit: **data goes in with textContent**. Use `innerHTML` only for HTML you typed into your own code, or `""` to empty an element. Also avoid `list.innerHTML += "
  • ...
    • "` in a loop: it turns the whole list back into text and rebuilds it every time, which is slow and throws away any click listeners already attached. **From an array to a list.** Data usually arrives as an array of objects. Loop over it and make one element per item: ``` for (const h of harvests) { const li = document.createElement("li"); li.textContent = `${h.farmer}: ${h.kg} kg`; li.dataset.farmer = h.farmer; // becomes data-farmer="Amina" list.appendChild(li); } ``` `dataset` stores small facts on an element as `data-*` attributes, so later code (a click handler, say) can tell which item it belongs to. You'll use that in the next unit. Put the building in a function that takes data and returns an element (`buildList(harvests)`). It's then easy to test, and the same function can draw a sensor log for a robot, a leaderboard for a game, or a stock list for a clinic.

notes: The data is a plain array of objects; the page is built from it.
makeItem makes, fills, styles and labels one element, and returns it.
textContent keeps typed-in text harmless; innerHTML would run it as HTML.
buildList loops and appends; nothing shows until the final appendChild onto the page.

exercises.title: One list item
exercises.prompt: Write a function makeItem(crop, kg) that creates an <li> element, sets its text to "CROP: KG kg" (for example "maize: 40 kg") using textContent, and returns it. Don't use innerHTML.

tests.name: HTML in the data stays as text
tests.hint_if_fail: Use textContent so the characters are shown exactly.

tests.why: Use textContent for data, not innerHTML.

exercises.title: A list from an array
exercises.prompt: Write buildList(harvests). harvests is an array like [{ crop: "maize", kg: 120 }, ...]. Return a new <ul> with one <li> per harvest, in order. Each li's text is "CROP: KG kg"; it gets the class "big" when kg is 100 or more; and li.dataset.crop is set to the crop name. An empty array gives an empty ul.

tests.name: big harvests are marked

hints: for (const h of harvests) { ... } and inside, make an li.
Don't forget ul.appendChild(li) inside the loop.

quiz.q: A name typed into a form is . Which line shows it safely?
quiz.why: textContent shows the characters; the others parse it as HTML and can run the code.

quiz.q: You create an li and set its textContent, but nothing appears on the page. Most likely?
choices: It was never appended with appendChild
quiz.why: A created element lives only in memory until you append it somewhere on the page.

quiz.q:
Why is list.innerHTML += "
  • ...
    • " inside a loop a poor habit?
choices: It rebuilds the whole list every time, is slow, drops listeners and is unsafe with data
It adds the items in reverse
quiz.why: Each += turns the list into text and rebuilds it from scratch.
dataset maps to data-* attributes (values are stored as text).

quiz.q: Why write buildList(data) that RETURNS an element, rather than code that writes straight into one fixed list?
choices: It can be tested on its own and reused for other data and other places
quiz.why: Functions that take data and return results are easy to test and reuse.

cards.a: textContent shows text exactly (safe for data); innerHTML parses HTML (only for your own markup).

explain: Explain why textContent is safer than innerHTML for showing a name someone typed, with an example name you make up.
